Perhaps I was misinformed, perhaps his chief services were connected with the collection of the Chinese tax which was in existence at that ti me, but I was "under the impression that he made himself generally useful in the customs and I can assure my friend that at Victoria and Vancouver these interpreters were necessary to the Customs Department.

I think the minister had bettter look into that. It seems iike an illustration of what I said a while ago that you get into a certain rut in the department and you go on voting and paying whether the business is going on or not. I cannot see why if the Customs Department want an interpreter it is not the business of the Customs Department to employ and pay him ? I imagine we paid them because of the large number of Chinamen coming in and that no doubt kept them employed ; now when you have a prohibitive tax you cannot need these men for the administration of the Chinese Act, so I should think the Prime Minister had better look into that and see whether that vote cannot be done away with. You pay $600 and $800, altogether $1,400 to collectors in connection with Chinese immigration. If your immigration tax is really prohibitive, and you are only getting in three or four Chinamen in the course of a year I do not think you can justify that vote. If the customs officers are not getting enough pay as customs officers, give it to them, but let the customs pay it, certainly they cannot have much to do in connection with Chinese immigration. That looks also like the survival of an old vote which there has not been enough energy in the minister of the department to revise. I must say again to my right bon. friend that we find it very inconvenient to have what ought to be a live department like the Department of Trade and Commerce administered from the dead house, so to speak, that is from the house that my friends opposite used to signify as the moribund house. It would be a great deal better in these live matters if we had the minister here. We have had examples of that this year. You cannot expect the Minister of Customs who has a large department to administer to bring these estimates down and show any know-ledge of them and he did not do that ; it is not to his discredit. The Minister of Finance is also a busy man or makes a pretense of being busy.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: It is the same thing.

About the same thing I suppose as far as his conscience goes. I think he has enough work to keep him going, and he cannot be expected to understand this department ; he cannot understand it unless he lives in it; and I would suppose you could take one of the supernumerary departments, such for instance-w-hen you get through this Autonomy Bill-as the Department of Justice ; you might put the Minister of Justice up there and bring the live department down here.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: He has had enough to do already.

Well he has to keep a check over the Department of the Interior and so long as that is run in the way it is I think it is well he is down here but we want to have the Department of Trade and Commerce down here also.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: I would have no objection to have the Department of Trade and Commerce here as it was before ; I would have no objection at all but I do not know that it is less effective because the head of the department has been transferred from one chamber to another. The only inconvenience is that the man who has to handle the estimates in this House cannot be so well supplied with the information to which the hon. gentleman is entitled. I am sorry I have not all the information because I learn myself as I go on in this matter. My hon. friend must not suppose that there are only three Chinamen who have come into Canada because only three have paid the capitation tax of $500. There are others, there are three classes of Chinamen and my hon,. friend will realize that when there is a population in our own country of 20,000 Chinamen and when they insist on going back to China during their life-because if they do not they must go back when they are dead,- there is necessarily a trade going on all the time. There are four classes of Chinamen, first of all there is the Chinaman who is subject to the capitation tax, that is to say on his first arrival when he comes here to work in Canada. Then there are Chinese who are living here, and are returning under registration to China. A certain number are registered, those who have their certificates and have paid their capitation tax. and they are entitled to go back to China for one year. Therefore there must be an examination of these men at the customs house, to see that they are the proper men they must be examined orally and their papers must be examined also, and therefore the services of the interpreter are required for that purpose. Then there is also the Chinaman in bond.
Dead or alive ?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
They are very much alive sometimes. We are a growing and progressive country and we do not import only goods in bond, but Chinamen also. We have to look after these men; they have to be carefully checked, because we do not want to mix our Chinamen with the American Chinamen, we must keep them separate. Then there is the Chinaman who is exempt altogether, the trader or the student who is above these little inconveniences, and for these reasons it has been found that the services of the interpreter were necessary. I am quite sure if my hon. friend had been here two years ago and had these estimates when the capitation tax was $100 and there was a pretty brisk trade in live flesh between this country and China, he would have had no fault to find with the employment of these two interpreters. Since that time the capitation tax has been increased, and it has almost prohibited that passenger trade. It was increased only two years ago. and my hon. friend I think cannot expect, and I do not think that on reflection he will insist, that the department should at once have cut off Mr. FOSTER.
its employees. We have to see how it will work out, and therefore perhaps it will be advisable in the future if the trade is so restricted-
Why do you need one at Vancouver, as well as at Victoria. Victoria must be the first port of call ?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: Some are landed at Victoria and some at Vancouver, There is a Chinatown in Vancouver and one in Victoria also.
Which is the first port of call ?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: Vancouver.

The right hon. gentleman referred to examining the Chinamen orally and also examining their certificates. As I understand it there is a further examination required. All Chinamen I think look very much alike.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: Hear, hear.
And in order to get over the difficulty you have to have measures as to the height. Ac., and these are recorded.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: These would require to be examined as well.
You will continue I suppose to measure them in the same way ?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: This can be done by somebody else than the interpreter. They are all carefully examined and marked.
I presume that the Chinamen who leave Vancouver or Victoria for China and return are remeasured, so as to make sure that others are not being smuggled in, in place of those who left.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: Yes. With regard to the item of $50,000 for commercial agencies, I suppose my hon. friend will expect me to give a statement of the agents and their localization. Mr. J. S. Larke is stationed at Sydney, Australia, D. H. Ross, at Melbourne, Australia, C. M. Kittson at Cape Town, South Africa. He was the representative of the Ogilvie Milling Company in South Africa for the last three years, and we appointed him on the death of Mr. Jar-dine. He is a Montreal man.
He devotes all his time to this V

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: Yes. A. F. A. Poindron is in Paris, France.
You have a commercial agent there besides Mr. Fabre ?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: Yes.
Why could not Mr. Fabre attend to this service ?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
Because I do not think Mr. Fabre, who is a success in

other directions, would be a success as a commercial agent. Mr. Poindron had been stationed in Montreal for a number of years in connection with Canadian trade, and is a very competent man. Mr. Fabre, as my hon. friend knows, is not at ail versed in commercial matters, and we thought it better to have a man who made trade his business.
How long has this gentleman been there ?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: Since the fall of 1902.
How often has he reported ?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: He reports regularly. I will give a statement by-and-by in regard to the reports of all the agents. The next is P. B. Ball, at Birmingham, Eng.; J. B. Jackson, at Leeds and Hull, Eng.
Has not my hon. friend ever had any thoughts as to whether this is an acceptable appointment for Canada or not ?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: I will come to that in a moment. I am now giving the list. P. B. MacNamara, at Manchester, Eng.; W. A. McKinnon, at Bristol, Eng.; Alex. MacLean, in Japan ; A. W. Donly, in Mexico ; C. E. Sontum, in Norway ; E. E. Burke, in Jamaica ; Edgar Tripp, in Trinidad ; S. L. Horsford, in St. Kitts ; R. Bryson, in Antigua. With regard to the system followed, this is the way it works. The Canadian commercial agents in various parts of the world are under the constant and direct supervision of the department at Ottawa.
What officer is in charge of them ?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: Mr. O'Hara. Their reports are forwarded regularly upon a very large variety of commercial and general topics of information. Their reports are carefully edited and promptly printed in the Weekly Report issued by the department. The Weekly Report is distributed free all over Canada to any persons interested.
How do you find out the persons interested ?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: By circulars and inquiries.
As a matter of fact, how many of these go out monthly 1

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: 1,150 every week.
How many are published ?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
About the same number. All commercial agents, when in receipt of trade inquiries, forward the same td the department and the inquiries are published in the Weekly Report. Parties in Canada requesting addresses of the same obtain them by return mail, upon applica-229
tion to the department. When an address is furnished a correspondent in Canada, the commercial agent is advised, so that he can notify his client of the name and address of the interested party in Canada. Uniform instructions have been sent to all the commercial agents, which has reduced their work to a systematic basis. A complete index of the Weekly Report is published every six months and sent to the regular recipients of the report. A comprehensive index of all the trade inquiries received from commercial agents is kept in the department.
With regard to Mr. Jackson's appointment, which I know has received some criticism, and as to which we had a debate in the House last year, I would like to read to my hon. friend the following letter :
The ' Trade Review ' Publishing Company,
687 Craig Street,
Montreal, Anril 22nd. 1905.
F. C. T. O'Hara, Esa.,
Superintendent of Commercial Agencies, Department of Trade and Commerce, Ottawa.
Dear Sir,-We take the liberty of congratulating you upon the splendid reports issued by the commercial agencies throughout Great Britain. It seems to us that you could make arrangements with trade publications in Canada for a larger issuance of the information contained in the reports, as we think it would be a good thing for the manufacturers in this country. We are satisfied in many instances the commercial agencies could be used direct by manufacturers to extend their trade in the various districts throughout Great Britain where your agents are located ; at any rate they could ascertain the possibility of doing business in their respective districts and thus save the manufacturers the necessity of incurring the expense of sending a representative there direct.
It seems to us that the manufacturers of this country are not availing themselves to the extent they might of the valuable information issued each week by the commercial agencies throughout Great Britain. You will observe in our issue of April 7th, on page 43, we publish in full the report of Mr. P. B. McNamara. At that time we also had at hand a report'from Mr. J. B. Jackson, which we would have given at length, but the space at our disposal did not allow us to do so.
We would simply say in conclusion, we have been closely following the reports issued by Mr. Jackson since he has received his appointment, and we are pleased to go on record as saying, said reports compare favourably with the reports issued by any of the American consuls throughout Great Britain, which we receive from week to week. We make this statement in reference to him because of the somewhat unfavourable criticism that was passed upon him at the time of his appointment. And we further make this statement for one who is and always has been a staunch Conservative, and believe it is only right that when an injustice is done an individual it is a duty to repair that injustice as far as possible.
We beg to remain Yours truly,
(Sgd.) HENRY' HARVEY & COMPANY, Proprietors ' Trade Review.'



With regard to the general work of the agencies, I would like to communicate to the House the following from the Canadian Manufacturers' Association :
Canadian Manufacturers Association.
Toronto, April 29, 1905. The Right Honourable
Sir Richard Cartwright,
Minister of Trade and Commerce.
Dear Sir,-I have the honour to inclose herewith a resolution adopted at the last meeting of the executive council of this asoooiation with reference to the commercial agency branch of the Department of Trade and Commerce.
Submitting the same for your consideration, I have the honour to be.
Your obedient servant,
(Sgd.) R. P. YOUNGE,
Secretary.
Resolution adopted at the regular meeting of the executive council of the Canadian Manufacturers Association, held at the head office, Toronto, on Thursday, April 20, 1905 :
Resolved, whereas, the Department of Trade and Commerce of the Dominion government has increased during the past year the usefulness of its commercial agency service :
(1)	By publishing the reports of the commercial agents and the foreign trade Inquiries weekly instead of monthly ;
(2)	By extending the scope of its work and appointing agents to new fields, and
(3)	By providing for more frequent visits to
Canada by its foreign agents in order that they may be kept familiar with Canada's increasing possibilities in export trade.	.
Therefore, be it resolved, that the Canadian Manufacturers Association express its appreciation and tender its best thanks to the Honourable the Minister of Trade and Commerce, for the assistance given to increase Canada's export trade by the development of the commercial agency service as above.

I have read many of the reports of our different commercial agencies, and in nearly every instance I have found complaint of tlie way goods were parcelled and shipped and of the state in which they arrive at their destination. This you find, for instance, in the reports of Mr. Larke. He has been in Australia for several years. I am not aware he has ever paid Canada a visit since he first went to Australia.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: He sails tomorrow for Canada.

It seems to me that if the commercial agents were brought home to Canada for an occasional trip, and, while here, addressed meetings in Toronto, Montreal and other important centres explaining to the people what is necessary in the shipment of their goods to the points in the territory for which the agent is appointed, it would do much to educate manufacturers and shippers on these points and so would overcome this difficulty. I believe that some organized body have already made this suggestion to the government. I am not sure, but it runs in my mind that that is the case.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council

speechtext:
Are these reports sent in weekly?
Sir WILFRID LAVK1ER. They are asked to report at least once a month and more frequently if they have anything to report.

I am not in a position to criticise very much the reports of the commercial agents, for I have not been receiving them. I would like the minister to ask that my name be put on the list of those to whom these weekly bulletins are sent so that 1 may see what is in them. We are paying about $45,000 for our Canadian agencies, so called; and the field covered is not as wide as it should he, even at that amount of money. In fact, our agents do not cover a very large territory. I see that there are none in the United States of America.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: I omitted one name. We appointed an agent in Chicago last March-Mr. Arnaud from Annapolis.
The United States consular service, although a poorly paid one, is most thorough.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: Hear, hear.

And I notice, in reading the United States consular reports, that those who make them take a great deal of pains in gaining and compiling information. They do not distribute themselves over a large area, with a paragraph referring to each thing, which is a very discursive and not very satisfying method. They take one particular subject at a time and make a thorough examination of it; and, when their report is sent in, their government has in it almost everything that can be said upon that subject. The Prime Minister will see what I mean if he will examine the United States consular reports. 1 notice that our reports are fragmentary-very fragmentary. For instance, take Mr. Jackson's report of May 3rd. He has four items. One is the trade of Bradford with the United States during the month of April; the second gives the trade of Huddersfield with the United States during the month of April ; the third gives the expenditure, income, &e., of the Leeds tramway; and the fourth notes that a good deal of dissatisfaction is being expressed as to the shipments of stale and over-kept bacon from the United States, and that Canadian bacon is steadily gaining ground. While all this is good information, I do not know that it is information that greatly stimulates the trade of Canada. It is a nice thing for a man to know just what the trade of Bradford with the United States in the month of April was, but it does not lead to anywhere. It is not merely *a fragment, but it is a mere point of a fragment. When you have got it read, there is not much of it that you can keep

or use. While such things may be good if they are well selected, I think it would be still better-it our men are capable of doing it; and I am sure that they are, many of them at least-if they would take up one subject of trade and make a thorough investigation of it and give all there is in it, so that those who read can make up their minds as to what field it opens if any, and whether they should go in to possess that field.
Further, the sending out of 1,100 copies of these reports each week is something ; but it is not very much. If you take the trouble to gather this information, tabulate it and print it, then, it seems to me you ought to give it a wider circulation. I suppose the present circulation is mainly among producers and shippers, but, no doubt, a good many of the 1.100 copies circulated go to persons not actively engaged in commerce. What the government ought to do is to get this information before the trading and producing public, and it might be worth while to consider whether means cannot be taken to give this information a wider distribution.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: What would my hon. friend (Mr. Foster) suggest?

I would suggest a little active propaganda. I would communicate with the members of parliament and ask them to give the names of manufacturers, producers and shippers in their constituencies to whom these reports could be sent. That is a thing that members would like to do, because they would like to have this information in the hands of those of their constituents who are interested. Then, boards of trade, manufacturers, associations and other bodies of that kind ought to co-operate. I daresay they do co-operate but that co-operation might be made more active. It may be worth considering whether the information could not be utilized in the trade papers. The point I make is that along with the fragmentary information. our agents ought to be asked to take up certain subjects so that the department here could make a thorough examination into the conditions. Take the fruit trade, the bacon trade, those are pretty well established, but there are other trades which are not, a lot of things we produce and that we want a market for.

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Conservative Party (1867-1942)
speechtext: Butter and cheese.

Yes, but these are pretty well developed now. But there are many other things for which we want to find a market. Now if they would take up these and make an exhaustive examination and put into brief form all the information there is, where the demand chiefly is, the prices paid, and everything of that kind with reference to any article of export, they would give very valuable information, which I 229*
think would be more useful than the fragmentary information now given.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: The suggestions of my hon. friend are very practical, and I am happy to tell him that in part they hare already engaged the attention of the government. I will ask the department to send my hon. friend the bulletins which have been issued in the past, and which will be issued. He will find In them something that will interest him.

There is another remark I would like to make. I have been led lately to question whether these monthly returns of exports and imports, and tabulations of trade, were fulfilling the object which the department had in view. Are they really read ? They are pretty bulky, they are a blue book, and there is a general disposition, when one gets a blue book, to throw it away somewhere. A blue book requires almost a technical education to understand it. A new member coming to this House knows what I mean. He gets a blue book, and he goes to an older member and says : Where am I to find out this thing? Well, it is in the book, but it requires a particular training to find and utilize it. If that is so with a new member of parliament, it is a great deal more so with a busy man outside. I have been led to question whether these monthly reports, coming out so long after the month in which they are dated, being so voluminous, and in part technical -whether they are not largely defeating the purpose we had in view, and whether better results would not be attained by the government in picking out certain points of interest and issuing a bulletin with reference thereto, putting the facts clearly so that the lay mind could understand them. I have been looking over some of these this morning, they are almost the size of a blue book, and they are incomplete. I doubt whether our commercial men freely read them. I would like to have the views of some commercial men here as to whether they do use them, whether they are of much value, whether it would not be better to take up some particular subject in the form Of a bulletin and present the statistics in regard to it.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: I would not like to give any opinion on the question raised by the hon. gentleman, in the absence of the Minister of Customs, under whose purview this subject comes.
The Department of Trade and Commerce issues them.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
I think they are prepared by the Customs Department, and issued by the Trade and Commerce. But I can say from my own knowledge that there is one class of the community which scans these reports very closely, and' I think would not like to have any change, and that is the manufacturers. To my certain know-

ledge they follow these reports very closely from day to day, from week to week and from month to month, in order to see in what line and in what direction trade is moving. As to the rest of the community, I have no personal knowledge how much interest is taken in them. I think my hon. friend from Leeds (Mr. Taylor) will corroborate me in saying that these reports are closely scanned by the manufacturers.

In comparing the reports of the Department of Trade and Commerce with those of the Customs Department, I find in a few instances that the figures do not agree. Now in the reports which have been referred to by my hon. friend from North Toronto (Mr. Poster), the title itself would lead one to suppose that the figures were not correct. That matter has already been brought up in the House this session, and the Minister of Customs stated that the figures were correct. If that is true, then why put in the title on these books the word ' unrevised.' That alone would lead the public to suppose that the figures were not as accurate as they might be.
The unrevised figures would have reference to the last month.

They are a monthly report, and the title would lead one to suppose that the figures are not vouched for by the department as being accurate. speechtext: As I have explained to my hon. friend last year, when the lead men came to us for assistance, representing that they had established an industry in British Columbia, which employed some 500 men in producing lead, that they had lost their market in the United States as the result of a combine there, and that unless we came to their assistance, the whole of the money which they had put into the industry would be wiped out and the men employed in it would be deprived of their work, I dare say they would have) preferred a duty to a bounty. AH the manufacturers of paint use our lead, and this is a growing industry, and a very rapidly growing industry, as my hon. friend knows. I do not say that in the way of forecasting events, but the matter is fairly open for consideration.

This is a very important branch of the service and perhaps my hon. friend would be interested to know in what manner the work of weighing and inspecting grain is performed. The inspection of grain in Canada has become from year to year a work of the greatest importance, constantly increasing and constantly necessitating improvements in the methods adopted to insure the reputation of Canadian grain in the foreign markets. There are two divisions at present under the Grain Act, which two divisions comprise the whole of Canada. The wrestern division with headquarters at Winnipeg and the eastern division with headquarters at Montreal. Mr. David Horn, until recently, was chief inspector of the western division, and Mr. Edward Craig was chief inspector of the eastern division. By an Order in Council, however, Mr. David Horn has been appointed chief inspector for the Dominion, so that the two inspection divisions as at present, and any future divisions which may be erected, may be brought into harmony throughout the Dominion. Upon the arrival of every grain train in Winnipeg, when it comes in, night or day, Sundays or holidays, a staff of grain men must be on hand so that samples may be taken from each car expeditiously in order that no train may be delayed. Mr. Horn has at Winnipeg a staff of from twenty' to thirty according to the season of the year ; six of these are duly examined deputy inspectors holding certificates. As soon as the train pulls in and the conductor hands in his way hill, the inspectors are allowed to make a list from it. With this list they go out to the track, open the cars as they come to them, according to the list. They usually go in gangs of three, that is to say, two samplers in charge of a deputy or foreman of experience. With a specially

contrived instrument lie stabs tbe grain in from seven to ten or a dozen places, and places eacli sample in a clotb on top of tbe grain at tbe door of tbe car. Tbe foreman mixes these various samples and satisfies bimself that it is a fair average of tbe car. This sample of about two pounds is tben placed in a bag, ticketed with tbe number of tbe car, &c. This sample is then taken to the grain inspection office and carefully examined by expert inspectors. A careful lookout is maintained for cars in bad condition, for leakages, &c. If any irregularities are discovered they are immediately reported. Tbe certificates are issued accordingly and the trains proceed to Fort William or Fort Arthur, the necessary documents being sent by mail to the grain inspection offices there. Samples of all tbe grain inspected are kept at the Winnipeg office. The system at present in vogue is found- to be eminently satisfactory, as is attested by the reputation of Canadian certificates in the foreign markets. The system at Montreal is very similar ; though at this point the work is not so heavy as it is in the west, and somewhat different from the large quantities of United States grain having to pass inspection at Montreal, whereas at Winnipeg the inspection is wholly of Canadian origin. I think the service has been performed satisfactorily. In so far as I know no complaints have been received against the men who do that work.

I think he is believed to be the best man in the Dominion of Canada for that purpose. That is the opinion both east and west in so far as I have been able to learn. In regard to the change in Toronto from Mr. Adamson to Mr. Campbell, did the government have any special reason for discharging Mr. Adamson? He was an officer who had occupied that position for some considerable time. Could the right hon. minister tell me if Mr. Campbell had any special quail-' fication ? The appointment was criticised somewhat in Toronto when the change was made.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: Mr. Adamson was dismissed upon the special recommendation of Mr. Horn. As to the qualification of Mr. Campbell, he passed the required examination and passed, I understand, one of the best possible examinations.
Where is the examination passed? What is the board?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
At Toronto.
The board of examiners which fixes the standards is the board which makes the examination.
Is there any record of the amount of grain examined at Winnipeg, Montreal or Toronto?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: My hon. friend will find the information in the report of the Department of Trade and Commerce, page 740.
This whole business amounts to $92,500. Who pays that ?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: There are specified fees charged for inspection and for weighing. I am informed that the capacity of a car has now so much increased that the government are contemplating almost duplicating the fees for weighing carload lots.
What amount of fees were collected last year ?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: Toronto produce grain inspection, $3,111.68 , Montreal, grain inspection and samples sold. $4,599.20 ; Manitoba inspection division, grain inspection, warehouse licenses and samples sold, $53,157.43.
According to that the government is in for about $30,000.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: Yes.
I should think that the grain business ought to pay for its own certificating.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: Hear, hear.
The government should see that the fees charged would cover the expenses.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: I have just said that we were contemplating increasing the fees.
In the meantime the country lost $30,000 last year.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: That fact has already engaged the attention of the government and it seems to be reasonable that the fees collected should be commensurate with the expenditure.

It is estimated that there will be 90,000,000 bushels of grain in the west this year. Our present inspecting staff costs us $95,000 a year and I would like to know if that same staff will be able to inspect the increased production. If so the chances are the receipts will double the expenditure.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: I cannot say as to that, but I suppose we will be guided by Mr. Horn, who the member for Halton (Mr. Henderson) states is a very competent man. He would no doubt be able to estimate in advance whether he will want any extra men or whether he can perform the service with the present staff. I have no doubt that the department will confer with Mr. Horn on the matter.
I understand the policy of the government is to make this business pay its own charges.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: I cannot say if that is the policy of the department, but I am of the same mind as my hon. friend (Mr. Foster) and think it would be my policy if I had charge.
It is the certificating that gives the character to and fixes the price of the grain ; it must be of great advantage to the trade as a whole and to the producer ultimately.
Under the Act of 1903 the Governor in Council had the right to fix the fees to be charged and I do not think that has been amended.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: We have the right.

I have only just come into possession of the correspondence which was brought down in response to a return moved for by me on the 22nd of February, in reference to the reasons why the nominations of the Montreal Board of Trade were not accepted on the Grain Survey Board named for Montreal. We were given to understand on the 27th of February, by the Prime Minister, that good and sufficient reasons for ignoring the recommendations of the Montreal Board of Trade would be found in this correspondence. The Prime Minister then said :
I do not mean that the fact that Messrs. Carruthers and Metcalfe were passed over would indicate anything against these gentlemen. I do not think it would he fair to imply or_ accept anything of that kind, but the Minister of Trade and Commerce informs me that these gentlemen have been passed over for good and sufficient reasons which will appear upon the face of the papers when they are brought down.
The papers have now heen brought down and although I have looked them over very carefully I can find no good and sufficient reasons given. The reasons are referred to in oue or two instances here. In a letter of the 4th of October addressed to the Right Hon. Sir Wilfrid Laurier, and signed, J. S. Norris & Co., a firm of Montreal grain shippers, these gentlemen call the attention of the government to the fact that great dissatisfaction exists in Montreal because the nominations made by the Montreal Board of Trade were not given effect to by the government. Mr. Norris writes :
Both Mr. Carruthers and Mr. Metcalfe have heen long identified with the grain trade here, and without doubt possess superior qualifications for acting on that board.
Turning to a letter of October 12th, which is a reply to this letter of Messrs. J. S. Norris & Co., by W. G. Parmelee, Deputy Minister of Trade and Commerce, I find this statement:	[DOT]

I do not propose entering into an argument upon the subject at all, but I know that your opinion is very different from the opinion of the Department of Justice to which the question was referred in the flrst instance. The decision of the department, as communicated to this office, is as follows :
Then follows the decision of the Department of Justice. In another letter of the 8th of October, signed W. G. Parmelee, Deputy Minister of Trade and Commerce, and addressed to the Right Hon. Sir Wilfrid Laurier, this statement is made:
The change in the personnel was not made without due consideration and it was deemed advisable that there should be a change, the reasons for which would take up too much space if enumerated.
It will be seen, therefore, that no reasons are given in the correspondence. Now, Sir, there are two questions involved in tills matter. The flrst question is :	The
slight which was offered to the Montreal Board of Trade by the government in making these nominations. Whether or not we accept the interpretation given to the Act by the Minister of Justice, the fact remains undisputed that on the 23rd of August. Mr. Parmelee wrote to the secretary of the board of trade as follows :
The Act of course provides for a recommendation by the board of trade of fit and skilful persons to compose the grain survey board, and the full provisions of the Act must be complied with before the new board is in a position to act. Your board will do well to make their recommendation so that they may be considered by the Governor in Council as early as possible.
And then, when the recommendations were made the reply which we received in Montreal was that the recommendations in a large measure shall not be adopted, that the government is not bound to adopt them and that the Minister of Justice has given an opinion to that effect: in fact that the recommendations might or might not have been made at ail, and yet the government would have felt perfectly free to go ahead with their nominations. The board of trade at the present day cannot see why they should be called upon to make any suggestions at all if their suggestions are to have such little weight with the government. but I cannot help feeling-and in this I know I voice the sentiments of the grain trade and the board of trade of Montreal-that there is some personal reason on the part of certain officials connected with the grain board at Ottawa or Montreal which has operated against the nomination of Messrs. Metcalfe and Carru-thers. and if we knew the whole facts it would be found that not so much the efficiency of the service is considered as certain private reasons that have not yet come out in the correspondence, and I think we ought to have some explanation that would be at least acceptable by the Montreal * Mr. AMES.
Board of Trade and the Montreal Grain Exchange, as to why Messrs. Metcalfe and Carruthers were not accepted when nominated.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: I take some exception to the first statement which has been made by my hon. friend, that the Montreal Board of Trade have reason to complain that the representations which they made to the government were not accepted in their entirety. I have only to observe to my bon. friend that the power of appointment rests upon the government and not upon the board of trade. The board of trade can do nothing but make suggestions.

Would it uot have been courteous to the Montreal Borad of Trade, in case any nominations which they made were not acceptable to the government, to have asked the Montreal Board of Trade to have made other nominations until a sufficient number of nominations were made to enable the government to choose a board which would be mutually satisfactory ?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
If my hon. friend asks me if it would not have been courteous for the department to ask the Montreal Board of Trade for other recommendations since the first ones had not been accepted, I think as a point of etiquette, although I ant not prepared to discuss it, there might be something in it. My point is that I do not accept the view of my hon. friend if I correctly understood his idea to be that the government was bound to accept the recommendations of the board. The government in this case has to consult somebody as to the making of the appointments, and I imagine there are no better parties to be consulted in a matter of this kind than the board of trade. But upon the advice that the government receives the government has to exercise its best judgment, and if for reasons sufficient for themselves they think the recommendations which have been made are not the wisest that couid have been made, if they have reason to take some exceptions to them, I think they are quite within their rights in not accepting them. As to the matter of courtesy I have nothing to say. I do not think it is a thing which after all amounts to very much if the relations have not been as tender and gentle as they might have been. I believe there is something in what my hon. friend says that there is an impression in Montreal-in some quarters, not everywhere-that there has been some bidden reason why the nominations of these two gentlemen have been passed over by the government. In addition to that my hon. friend says : We are entitled to know what these reasons are ; the government are not expected to act on caprice or by whims, and if they passed over the recommendation of a respectable body like the Board of Trade of Montreal they must have had

some reasons for that and we should know them. The government of course must accept the responsibility of their action, and I do not know but I presume that if the government have passed over the names of these two gentlemen and substituted two other names, who 1 think are vei-y competent, they had some reason for that. There could be no reason at all why the action of the government should not be scrutinized in every way. My hon. friend thinks we ought to know these reasons ; I have only to say that I cannot give him the reason at this moment. When my hon. friend brought the matter up on January 27, I called upon the Minister of Trade and Commerce and reported to him the views which had been expressed by my hon. friend when I saw his notice on the order paper, and the Minister of Trade and Commerce told me then that he had good and sufficient reason for the action which he had taken. I shall be happy to confer with the.Minister of Trade and Commerce again and I shall be happy to discuss the matter with my hon. friend (Mr. Ames) at a later stage, and to give the reasons which have actuated the department in the action of which he complains.

1 think it.would be in the general interest of the grain trade and of that harmony which should prevail between the government and commercial bodies if the matter should be a little more thoroughly ventilated. There is a feeling-how just it may be we do not know-which is not entirely one of satisfaction with the local officials connected with the grain inspection of Montreal. I have myself been in receipt of considerable correspondence from grain importers in Great Britain making severe criticism on the grain inspection officials of the city of Montreal, and there is a feeling that the government was influenced to some extent in their action in this matter by the fact that those nominations were not acceptable to certain officials stationed at Montreal in connection with the grain trade.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
All I can say >at this moment is that if there are any reasons to suspect any official of the government at Montreal It would be the duty of my hon. friend to give his reasons, not here, but to the department so that the department may fake action if it deem it advisable. I have had, so far as I am concerned, no complaint against any official, but if there are some officials who are under suspicion it is not fair that they should be held under suspicion. The matter should be investigated and if they are found guilty they should be removed from the service, but if they are not guilty their record is clear and nothing more should he heard of the charges. I think my hon. friend will find when I give them the reasons and the documents upon which the government has acted that perhaps he will have cause to change
his mind as to the reasons which have influenced the government.
Possibly.

On this point I regret that I have not the wording of the statute before me, but my impression is that when we passed this Act last year provision was made that the Board of Trade of Montreal and the Board of Trade of Toronto should recommend to the government the persons that might be appointed to these positions. I certainly for one- and I attended meetings on 10 or 11 days of a sub-committee examining the whole Act but my impression is that we intended to provide that out of these recommendations the government should make the selection of inspectors, and I am somewhat surprised to learn from the member for Montreal (Mr. Ames) that this lias not been carried out, that the government, for some reason 'which the Prime Minister has not made known, had gone outside apparently of the recommendations. I think certainly that if there was any good reason why these men should not be appointed, it is just as well the country should know it, because there has been, as my friend (Mr. Ames) has said, for some time a suspicion that; everything was not right in connection with Montreal inspection; in fact it was not acceptable in the old country at all. That was the reason why I asked the right hon. gentleman with respect to whether or not complaint had been made during the past year in that regard. I was very glad indeed to hear that the difficulty complained of here had been removed, but it seems that there are still some inquiries with respect to the same thing. Whether it is owing to some particular officials there not being acceptable or not discharging their duties properly, for my part I am entirely unable to say, but I would say that it is of the utmost importance to all grain shippers that complete confidence should be established in Montreal grain inspection, not only among the people of this country but more especially among the people of the old country who are receiving the shipments of grain. Had the government followed the course laid down in the Act, and named the men recommended by the Board of Trade, I think ft would have tended to remove a good deal of the difficulty, that seems to have prevailed in the last year or two, and have established complete confidence both in the old country and in this country. But it would seem as if political or some other influence had prevailed, and no doubt the shippers and the receivers of goods from the old country will still be under the impression that tire right men are not in the right place.

May I say a word in reply to my hon. friend from Halton ? He has,
I think, to a slight extent misunderstood my remarks. So far as the individual gen-

tlemen are concerned, the nominees of the government are perfectly satisfactory. The only question at issue was that the Montreal Board of Trade thought that the government could only act on their recommendation.
I thought so too.

That is certainly what any layman would read in the law, and the board of trade were considerably chagrined at having been invited to make nominations and having their nominations turned down. They thought they should at least have been asked to make new nominations, because, without disputing the power of the government to make the appointments, they thought that the nominations should first come from the board of trade. But I wish ic to be understood that we have no criticism to make of the personnel of the board. The gentlemen composing it at present are in every way fitted for the duties they are called on to perform.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: I would further say that when the government received the communication of the board of trade, the Minister of Trade and Commerce thought he was bound to take exception to two of the names recommended, and he did so. But he was of the same opinion as the hon. member for Halton and the non. member for Montreal, that the government could not go outside of the recommendations of the board of trade ; and it was to clear up that point that he asked the opinion of the Minister of Justice, who advised him that he was not bound to take the recommendations of the board of trade, but that those recommendations were merely sent to them as a means of attaining an end, and that he could exercise ms own judgment, which he did. I am glad to have from the hon. member for Montreal his confirmation of the fact that no exception can be taken to the gentlemen appointed.

Allow me to put one further question. Supposing a British shipper of grain is desirous of having samples of the standards that are fixed on this side of the water, in order to enable him to purchase by letter rather than by sample, can he on demand obtain such samples practically free of charge ?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: I am informed that he can. He can have those in England without applying in Canada at all, because all the samples, when determined in Canada, are sent to England.

That does not quite meet the case, which I have in mind, the case of a large flour milling firm in Cardiff, Wales, who import large quantities of wheat, including Canadian wheat. Thev recentlv applied to the department in 'Montreal for samples of grain, and received a very curt reply from the local inspector to the*effect Mr. AMES.
that there were no samples of the kind of grain they asked for. I transmitted this letter to the department, who I know appreciate the situation. What I wish to know is whether this Cardiff miller can secure samples direct from Canada; because it is probable that the samples in possession of the British exchange could not be divided for the purpose of distributing them among several millers. Would it be possible for this large milling concern-and it is greatly in the interests of Canada that they should purchase largely Canadian wheat-to produce direct from Canada their own samples of the current standards of wheat, corn and other grain ?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
I am sorry to say that I cannot give my hon. friend the information to-day, but I will have the matter inquired into, and have it given to him officially.
Culling timber,, $17,100.
How many of these cullers are there now ?

And what are their duties ?
Sir tvILFRID LAuRIER. At present there are six.
Are they located chiefly in Quebec ?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: They are located in Quebec. The trade which necessitated these cullers is more and more diminishing, and it will not be very long before the office will have to be abolished altogether. The position of superintendent is vacant, and we have not filled it. In fact, I think the department has prepared a Bill for next session, with a view to dealing with this subject.
What is the object of this culling ?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: It is to measure the square timber coming to the harbour of Quebec for exportation, and to give certificates of measurement. If there is a dispute between the purchaser and the vendor as to the quantity, it is customary to have the culling done ; or if a man brings a raft down and wants to have an official statement of the measurement of the timber in it, he obtains it from the cullers. These are the principal services which they render.
Is Quebec the only port where this is done ?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: Yes. It was formerly a very important office.
Why do the owners of the timber not pay for the measurement of it ? Why is it charged to the government ?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: My bon. friend bas asked me more than I can explain. 1 can only say that it lias been so for fifty years.

In, St. Jobn and everywhere else, so far as I know, there are sworn surveyors, and the expense is paid by the owners of the timber ; and one would think that would be followed in all the cities and ports.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: The office of the cullers has been in existence for some fifty years, and at one time I believe it was thought to be an absolute necessity. That was at a time when millions of square timber were shipped from Quebec every year. 1 remember-I think it was 1S76-the lumbermen who were then in the House agreed and pressed upon the government the diminution of the number of cullers. A certain number were superannuated, each receiving a pension of $200 a year. This year, the amount asked for pensions is diminished by $200 as one of these gentlemen has died. I think we may have here a precedent to dispose of the other cullers in the same way. My impression is, as representing the city of Quebec, that the time has about arrived when we should do something with regard to that office, either to completely abolish it or to re-east it on some other plan.

I notice that the government ask for the same amount-$4.200- as last year, notwithstanding the fact that one of the cullers has died.
Sir WILFRID LAURIER, The amount for the payment of cullers is the same, $4,200, but the amount for superannuated cullers, which was $4,200 last year, is reduced fh $4,000 because of the death of one of these superannuated cullers.
Public works-chargeable to income-harbours and rivers-Nova Scotia, $387,260.

Is it the intention of the government to proceed to-night and put through all the items covered by this large vote ? We are almost defenceless on this side of the House ; we are scarcely equal to the occasion. I trust the minister will not press these matters in view of the fact that we have no Minister of Public Works in the House. I have no doubt he hopes to have one within two or three days. But in the absence of the Minister of Public Works we can hardly hope for a full explanation of these votes. Having adjourned early last night and the night before, I think we might follow in the same line, and not proceed to deal with an important vote like this with so few members present. The works represented in this list of items are scattered all, over Nova Scotia. And, the opposition not Jiaving a single representative from Nova Scotia, will be obliged to get its information from some other source than its
own members. So, it cannot be expected that we can duly criticise these items with such a thin House. I trust the minister will not take advantage of our weakness on this occasion and try to press through so many items as are covered by this vote.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: There is no disposition to press these matters unduly. We have been getting along very pleasantly with our estimates-we certainly have no reason to complain. I would suggest that this item should not be proceeded with to-night. At the same time 1 would not like to accept the suggestion of the hon. gentleman (Mr. Henderson) that we should not proceed with any of these items unless the Minister of Public Works is in his seat. We may find it necessary, in order to keep the business of the House moving, to take up some of these votes. But, if there is any item that any hon. gentleman wishes held over, that can be done. Instead of taking up Public Works we might take up some miscellaneous items not of so controversial a character as the vote for Public Works. A number of these are merely formal votes, and, I think, will not require any particular explanation. If there is any item that is objected to, we will let it stand. And, in any case we will have an early adjournment.
In half an hour.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
All right. If, on any of these items, the information is not ready, yet, as these matters are of a formal character, the committee might be good enough to let the items pass with the understanding, that, on the supplementary estimates, further information will be given if desired.
Miscellaneous-Academy of Arts, $2,000.
I thought that was disposed of.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: It is not marked as passed. This is the usual grant to the Royal Canadian Academy of Arts. It is for the encouragement of the fine arts, and is paid to the president of the Royal Canadian Academy.

In Toronto ?
. ' [DOT]

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: The Royal Canadian Academy holds its exhibition in different parts of the country. I think Toronto is the headquarters.

I do not know whether the Minister of Finance (Mr. Fielding) is able to give me the information I desire, yet, in case he may be, I will put a question. Is it intended to introduce this session an amendment to the Criminal Law with relation to Art Unions incorporated in the old country, which are at present forbidden by our criminal law to carry on their operations in Canada ? I understood from the Minister of Justice (Mr. Fitzpatrick) that he would

speakerposition: subtopic
stagedirection
speechtext:
'mo
introduce this session an amendment -which would allow art unions incorporated in the old country and known to he of high class, to do business in Canada.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
I am sorry I cannot give my hon. friend (Mr. Daniel) a definite answer. I am heartily in sympathy with the view he expresses. I am familiar with the subject, for it was called to my attention when I was in the old country by gentlemen of high standing connected with the Art Union. The difficulty is to draft a clause which will distinguish between genuine art unions having for their object the encouragement of art, and other concerns that are mere lotteries. My hon. friend from St. Antoine division, Montreal (Mr. Ames) will remember that there were a number of institutions operating in Montreal under the guise of art unions which did a good deal of harm. In the effort to suppres these it appears we have shut out bona fide organizations. Now, all over the country there will be found genuine objects of art which have been distributed under their system, and no harm has come, but on the contrary much good, by supplying the homes of Canada with line pictures at a moderate cost. I sympathize with the view that we should endeavour to get a form of words which wTouId allow bona fide art unions to be formed without admitting the mere lotteries. But up to the present time there has been a difficulty in getting a form of words which would serve a good purpose without at the same time admitting evil. I will remind the Minister of Justice of the matter again to see if we can carry out the object which I think the most of us will concur in.
Grant to the imperial government to cover Canada's proportion of probable losses in connection with the operation of the Pacific cable, $125,000.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: This cable is a joint concern between the imperial and colonial governments, and this is the proportion of the loss which is chargeable to Canada. This is an estimate made of wbat the loss is likely to be. We had to pay a sum in a previous year, I do not exactly remember the amount, but I think It corresponds with this, and this estimate is based upcfn past experience.

In any case, this item is one which we are in honour bound, at least to pay, whatever it may be. The amount is determined, I understand, at the end of the fiscal year, and we pay directly to the imperial government.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: AVe pay to the commission, and the imperial government is the centre. It is an obligation, the proportion of Canada is fixed. The exact amount is not fixed, because that is a matter of business at the close of the year.
What is Canada's proportion ?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I would not risk saying, lest I make a mistake.
Does Australia pay any proportion and what 1

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Yes, the various colonies pay in proportion to their interest, as laid down in the arrangement. They are to he charged with the sum which will represent their share of the earnings, and of course they would share in the profits, if there were any.
It seems to me, either that this cable is badly managed, or else it was not necessary. There seems to be something radically wrong in the whole concern.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Well, it was thought to he necessary as a part of a large colonial policy in which we must take a little risk. Probably it has been somewhat disappointing financially, but all these important undertakings, in their early stages, are apt to involve some loss. But we hope to do better. My hon. friend Is aware that the Postmaster General has just left for the old country in order to be present at a conference in relation to this matter, and we hope that some better arrangement may be made. However, as my hon. friend from Montreal (Mr. Ames) says, we are obligated to pay our proportion, whatever it may he, and this is the estimated amount required for that purpose.

I do not object to pay anything that we are really and in duty bound to pay. But I would like to have a statement of the whole cost of the business. It would be much more satisfactory, before voting this large amount of money, to have the whole statement on the ' Hansard ' so that members of the House may become familiar with the transaction.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: This is a large item, and my hon. friend's criticism is so reasonable that, if it is his wish that this item should stand, I will offer no objection.
When may we have the information ?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Very soon.
Will it be given before six o'clock on Monday ? I am here generally all the rest of the week.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I will promise not to .give it before six o'clock on Monday.

issued representing the capital outlay. Interest lias to be paid on that capital, and also working expenses. There is found to be a deficiency and this is Canada's estimated proportion.

terms, because it was looked upon as an imperial undertaking.

of interest, as we think, the rate of interest they demand.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I think that is one of the points in dispute. My recollection is that we are only paying 4 per cent, but their intention is that it should stand on a par with provincial subsidies, and that the interest should be 5 per cent.

That was my impression. about one-sixth. * In that event, the entire loss would be about three-quarters of a million dollars. I have no desire to prolong the discussion. The member for Lennox (Mr. Wilson), however, would like to have further information.
